Effect of the amount of urea added on 
Collard Greens (Brassica oleracea) plant 
growth 
Plant the Moon Challenge | Fall 2023 | Professional/Undergraduate Division 
 
Minnesota West Bluejays | Team # 16178 
Minnesota West Community & Technical College 
Worthington, MN 
 
Grace Barber, Ashley Freese, Sierra Goedtke, Maelie Holt, Cathy Diaz, Claire Mahlberg, Ethan 
Meyer, Casey Miller, Solomon Mitchell, Dawson Svalland, Sahyra Talamantes, Tryee Watkins, 
Dr. Tyler Wadzinski, and Heidi Tarus 
 
Grant Funded by NASA’s Minnesota Space Grant Consortium

P a g e | 1 
 
Introduction 
This project focuses on addressing the human need of access to nutritious food that can 
be grown on the Moon as human look toward colonization of various celestial bodies. In order 
for plants to be grown for food, they need access to water and essential nutrients including 
potassium, phosphorus, and nitrogen. Prior studies show that most plant essential nutrients are 
available in the composition of lunar regolith with the exception of useful nitrogen (Wamelink 
et al., 2014). Nitrogen is an essential macronutrient for plants and is used in the synthesis of 
proteins, nucleic acids, and some vitamins needed for growth (Clark et al., 2018). Prior research 
done by the Fall 2022 and Spring 2023 Minnesota West Bluejays research team, demonstrated 
that addition of a nitrogen source (either ammonium nitrate, calcium nitrate tetrahydrate, or 
urea) caused more plant growth over no nitrogen; however, the three nitrogen sources were 
not significantly different from each other. Both teams suggested using urea as a nitrogen 
source as it provides the highest mass percent of nitrogen requiring only 2.1 g of compound per 
gram of nitrogen delivered (48% nitrogen), which makes it a preferred nitrogen source in regard 
to reducing spacecraft payload mass. This team is interested learning more about how the 
amount of urea added during experimental set-up influences plant growth. The main driving 
question for this project is to discover the trade-off between limiting the mass of urea fertilizer 
brought to the moon while producing the highest yield of nutrient rich crops needed to feed 
individuals living on the moon. 
Theory 
The amount of urea added to the pots (independent variable) was based on results from 
the Fall 2022 and Spring 2023 Minnesota West Bluejays research teams. The treatments were 
picked by utilizing the suggested fertilizing loading rate of 0.5 lb N per 1000 ft2 (Swift &

P a g e | 2 
 
Hammond, 2020) that was used in the research done last year. There will be four treatments: 
no urea, half dose of 0.013 g urea per pot, suggested dose of 0.026g urea per pot, and one and 
a half dose of (0.039 g urea per pot). Urea has the highest mass percent of nitrogen and only 
requires 2.1 g of compound per gram of nitrogen delivered, which makes it the most preferred 
nitrogen source in regard to reducing rocket payload mass. However, urea must go through a 
three-step process where it is converted to ammonia, then ammonium, and then nitrate before 
plants can use it (Mengel, n.d). Additionally, urea is water soluble prior to being converted, 
making it susceptible to leaching. A benefit of urea is that it can be locally sourced and 
extracted from urine produced by individuals living on the moon. 
The team decided to plant Collard Greens (Brassica oleracea) because of the fast 
germination time of four to seven days, its ability to grown at lower temperatures between 4-
18 degree Celsius (40-65 degrees Fahrenheit), its ability to continuously provide highly 
nutritious leafy greens over a long period of time once mature (Palomo, 2021). B. oleracea is a 
dicot plant that contains high nutrient content in the leaves. According to the U.S. Department 
of Agriculture (2019), one cup of chopped raw collard greens (36g) contains 11 calories, 1g of 
protein, 1.44g of fiber, 2g of carbohydrate, and less than 1g of fat and sugar. In addition, B. 
oleracea are an excellent source of many essential vitamins and minerals for humans including 
Vitamin A, Vitamin C, Vitamin K, calcium, potassium, folate, and antioxidant (Baby, n.d). The 
leaves can be eaten raw or cooked allowing for the plant to provide versatility and diversity in 
the types of food individuals can create using the plant. Another reason this plant was picked 
was due to the high success rate of the Collard Greens plant growth in the Fall 2022 research 
experiment.

P a g e | 3 
 
 
The data collected in the experiment (dependent variables) will include the primordial 
leaf emergence for germination rate, the number of true leaves, the length of the largest leaf, 
and the pH of the soil. 
We hypothesize that Collard Greens (B. oleracea) grown in the pots containing the most 
amount of nitrogen will produce the most leaves and have the largest leaves indicating the 
highest amount of plant growth. 
Experiment & Measurement Methods 
Initial Set-Up 
The treatments were picked by utilizing the suggested fertilizing loading rate of 0.5 lb N 
per 1000 ft2 (Swift & Hammond, 2020) that was used in the research done last year. There will 
be four treatments: no urea, half dose of 0.013 g urea per pot, suggested dose of 0.026g urea 
per pot, and one and a half dose of (0.039 g urea per pot). Each treatment will have 8 replicates 
(see Figure 1). Each pot (7cm x 7cm x 7.7cm) contained the same soil composition of 50% top 
soil and 50% lunar regolith by volume. Each pot was watered with 25ml of water. 
The larger team of 12 students formed six sub-teams that contained two students per 
team. The other two sets of posts measured by the team coach. Each sub-team was responsible 
for one pot per treatment. The pots were identified by a colored popsicle stick placed in the 
back of the pot with the team’s name written on it. The eight team names were HLT-1, HLT-2, 
CS Party, ST, CA, ED, SM, and CG. The team planted each treatment pot with three Collard 
Greens (Brassica oleracea; Gardeners Basics Non-GMS Heirloom Seeds) seeds and watered with 
25ml of tap water. Over the course of the eight-week grow period, the set-up was kept indoors

P a g e | 4 
 
with a temperature of 22°C with the set of pots placed under a grow light containing 2-18” GE 
plant and aquarium bulbs on a 12-hour light: 12-hour dark timer. The grow light was placed 12 
cm from the top of the pots (Image 1). 
 
 
 
 
Figure 1. Diagram of experimental set-up showing the four treatment groups each with eight 
replicate pots for a total of 32 pots.

P a g e | 5 
 
Image 1. Pictures of the initial plant growth set-up on September 26, 2023. 
Plant Care 
Each pot was top watered with 25ml of distilled water on Tuesday and Thursday each 
week during the grow period. All pots were watered on the same schedule independent of the 
presence of seedling or no seedlings. According to the seed packet, the B. oleracea should be 
thinned to be at least 30.48 cm (12 inches) apart; therefore, as the pots are 7cm in width, the 
plants were thinned to one seedling on October 17, 2023 by keeping the tallest plant in the pot. 
Thinning is a common practice in gardening and was done to give the tallest (strongest) 
seedling in each pot the best chance to grow. The plants were kept in the same room through 
the duration of the experiment and were moved away for the light source for a maximum of 30

P a g e | 6 
 
minutes on Tuesday at 1pm to take measurements and then replaced back in the same location 
after measuring. 
Measurements 
 The dependent variables for this experiment were primordial leaf emergence for 
germination rate, number of true leaves, length of longest leaf, and pH of the pots. Primordial 
leaf emergence was used to collect data on germination rate of the plants. Germination rate 
was collected once by visually observing of the number of germinated seeds 14 days after 
planting. The soil pH measurements and plant height measurement were collected by sub-team 
members once a week each on Tuesday using the soil pH meter sent with the lunar regolith an 
a 15-cm ruler. 
In addition, a top-view and side-view picture of the entire set-up was taken once a week 
on Tuesday after watering the pots (Appendix B: Photos). Records of the data collected was 
kept on paper next to the set up and was entered each week into a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet 
each week for data analysis. 
Analysis & Results 
Data for each sub-team was written down on paper data collection sheets and entered 
into a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet each week. The paper data collection sheets were stored in 
the biology lab and electronic copies of the data was stored on Tarus’ laptop computer. The 
data was organized and graphed using Microsoft Excel. Statistical tests for the means, standard 
errors, Shapiro-Wilk tests for normality, and the Kruskal Wallis H tests were performed using 
the free online website Statistics Kingdom (https://www.statskingdom.com/).

P a g e | 7 
 
Soil pH & Germination Rate 
The soil pH of each pot did not change significantly over the course of the eight weeks 
and stayed at a pH of 8 (Appendix A Table 4). Because the pH did not change over time 
statistical analysis was not done on this data. The germination (primordial leaf emergence) data 
collected shows that the seeds had a mean ± standard error germination rate of 37% ± 16% in 
the control group, 71% ± 10% in the half dose group, 54% ± 11% in the full dose group and 50% 
± 15% in the dose and a half group (Appendix A Table 1 and Figure 2). 
Figure 2. Box plot with whiskers showing the effect of the amount of urea on average 
germination rate (primordial leaf emergence). Each treatment group contained eight pots (N 
= 8) where three seeds were planted per pot. 
 
 
 
A Shapiro-Wilk tests showed a significance departure from the normality for the control 
group, W(8) = .78, p = .024 and the dose and a half group, W(8) = .81, p = .044; however, there

P a g e | 8 
 
was not a significant departure from normality for the half dose group, W(8) = .84, p = .076 or 
the full dose group, W(8) = .91, p = .362. Because the data did not show normality for all four 
groups, a Kruskal-Wallis H test was used to analyze the between group data. The Kruskal-Wallis 
H test indicated that there was a non-significant difference in the germination rate between the 
four groups, χ2(3) = 2.77, p = .428, with a mean rank score of 13.13 for the control group, 20.56 
for the half dose group, 16.38 for the full dose group, 15.94 for the dose and a half group. 
Plant Growth 
 
The data for the number of true leaves and the length of the longest leaf can be viewed 
in appendix A Table 2 and Table 3, respectively. The number of plants that survived over the 8-
week experiment was not high enough to give a sample size where statistics could be done. The 
high mortality rate of the plants is addressed in the discussion and conclusion section. 
Discussion & Conclusion 
We hypothesized that Collard Greens (B. oleracea) grown in the pots containing the 
most amount of nitrogen would produce the most leaves and have the largest leaves indicating 
the highest amount of plant growth. Data from the experiment did not supported the hypothesis due 
to the high mortality rate of the plants over the course of the 8-week experiment. The plants in this set-
up were stacked on top of each other (Image 1) with no heat barrier between the bottom light and the 
top flat of plants. This could have caused the plants on the top to dry out quickly which was not 
observed until week 4 of the experiment when most of the plants died in the full dose treatment group 
and the dose and a half treatment group. In addition, a compound to help with water retention was not 
added to the soil mixture which caused the plants to dry out quickly. The effect of the extra nitrogen 
could have also been a factor as well as overfertilizing can cause fertilizer burn which causes burned 
leaves and wilting and drooping plants (Planta, n.d). The experiment did show that there was no

P a g e | 9 
 
significant difference between the treatment groups and the primordial leaf germination rate. This 
indicates that the amount of nitrogen added to the soil did not affect germination rate. 
The overall goal of the project was to see if reducing the amount of urea added to the 
soil could still produce abundance plant growth while reducing the payload on the spacecraft. 
Based on prior research, the team recommends the use of urea as a nitrogen source when 
growing as urea is the most weight efficient nitrogen source tested in this experiment. In 
addition, the requirement to bring urea from Earth of the Moon may not be needed as urea can 
potentially be extracted from the urine of humans living on the Moon. Human typically produce 
12 to 20 g of urea in urine over the course of 24-hours (Jacob, 2021). Depending on the number 
of humans and the nitrogen requirements of the plants being grown, this amount of urea could 
be sufficient to avoid bringing urea to the Moon. Investigations into the method and efficiency 
of urea extraction from human urine is needed. 
Future Research 
In addition, to future research discussed above the following areas are suggested for 
future research. The urea was added during the initial set-up, so experiments looking at the 
reapplication of urea fertilizer and its influence plant growth should be investigated. This is 
especially significant for urea since this compound is susceptible to leeching quickly from the 
soil. In addition, nitrogen is important in building the enzyme ribulose-1-5-bisphosphate 
carboxylase-oxygenase (RuBisCO) which is the enzyme used during carbon fixation in the light-
independent reaction during photosynthesis. A future study could measure the photosynthetic 
rate of the plants as a measure for nitrogen uptake in the plants. Finally, the team suggests 
replicating the set-up used during this experiment as this experiment failed due to the low 
sample size due to the plants not surviving.
